**My reasoning as this farmer:**

I've been farming this land in Quzhou my whole life. Around here, everyone does winter wheat followed by summer maize — that's just how it's done on the North China Plain. The land is flat, we have wells for irrigation, and the county extension station has always supported this rotation. I'm not going to change that at 65.

I have 10 mu of contracted land. All of it goes into the wheat-maize rotation. My son is in Handan City, so I manage most of it myself, hiring machine operators for planting and harvesting — my back can't take the old way anymore.

For wheat, I'll use an improved variety the seed shop recommends — probably a Jimai or Kenong line, not too new. I know how to manage them. I'll do rotary tillage with a hired tractor in early October, apply base fertilizer, then sow. Three irrigations — one before sowing to ensure germination, one at jointing in March, one at heading in May. I'll spray herbicide in autumn and a combined fungicide-insecticide at heading to protect against rust and aphids.

After wheat harvest in June, I go straight into maize with no-tillage — just direct seed into the stubble. Everyone does this now, saves time and money. Hybrid seed, definitely — Zhengdan 958 or whatever the shop has. Summer rain usually handles irrigation but I'll pump once if July is dry. One herbicide pass after emergence, one insecticide for corn borer in August.

I use more nitrogen than the extension station says I should, but I've always done it this way and my yields are decent. No reason to change now.

I apply nitrogen at rates slightly above official guidelines because experience tells me yields drop noticeably when I cut back, and I cannot afford a poor harvest. I irrigate wheat three times to ensure establishment and protect the two critical yield stages, and maize only once since summer monsoon rainfall usually suffices. I use rotary tillage for wheat to prepare a good seedbed, but no-tillage for maize to save cost and time — a practice I adopted after neighbors showed it works. Two pesticide applications per crop cover the main threats: weeds early and disease or insects at key growth stages. I hire machinery for all mechanized operations since I can no longer do heavy field work myself."
